entities.name: Mei Bo
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Mei Bo, a revered Grand Tutor (Taishi) of the late Shang dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BCE), stands as a paradigmatic figure of loyal opposition and tragic martyrdom in early Chinese history. His unwavering moral stance against the tyrannical rule of Di Xin, more commonly known as King Zhou of Shang, positioned him as a symbol of integrity and a precursor to the virtuous officials who would challenge corrupt power throughout subsequent imperial eras. His fate, inextricably linked to the downfall of the Shang, underscores the intense political and ethical conflicts that characterized the transition from Bronze Age hegemonies to the nascent Zhou feudal system.

Mei Bo's historical narrative is primarily preserved in foundational texts like the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian) and the *Fengshen Yanyi* (Investiture of the Gods), which depict his staunch remonstrance against King Zhou's increasingly debauched and cruel governance. He vociferously condemned the king's excesses, including the construction of the "Deer Terrace" and the use of the "Paoluo" (bronze pillar punishment). His persistent criticism, rooted in traditional Shang moral codes, ultimately provoked King Zhou's wrath. According to legend, Mei Bo was subjected to the horrific "minced meat" punishment (醢), a public execution designed to terrorize and silence dissent within the Shang court.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Mei Bo's martyrdom was a pivotal event that provided moral justification for the Zhou conquest of the Shang, profoundly shaping the Mandate of Heaven concept and establishing an enduring archetype of loyal opposition in Chinese political thought.
